text: Last lesson made the case for writing decisions down at all. This one gets concrete: the actual four-part format, and a complete worked example written the way you'd really commit it to a repository, so you can see exactly what belongs in each section and what a reader loses when a section gets skipped.

Every real ADR has the same four sections. Context is the problem that forced a decision to be made — without it, a reader can't tell whether the original problem still applies today. Options Considered lists the real alternatives, including whichever ones were rejected and why. Decision is one unambiguous sentence, no hedging. And Consequences records what followed — the benefits you were going for, and the downsides you accepted to get them.

Here's Context from a real ADR this course already set up back in Chapter 3: a platform expanding to three regions needed one chokepoint for shared firewall, DNS, and egress enforcement, without the peering relationships growing out of control through a full mesh between every spoke.

And here's the Decision and Consequences that followed: hub-and-spoke, one hub per region, every spoke's traffic forced through that hub's firewall. Notice the Consequences section states the downside in writing — the hub becomes a throughput bottleneck to monitor, and spoke-to-spoke traffic picks up an extra hop of under two milliseconds. That's what makes it a real record of a tradeoff instead of a justification written after the fact.

Three ways ADRs commonly fail despite looking complete. A Decision with no Context leaves a reader unable to tell if the original problem still exists. Listing only the chosen option isn't Options Considered, it's just restating the Decision twice. And a Consequences section that's all upside means the tradeoff either wasn't real, or wasn't honestly written down — every meaningful decision has some real cost.

Next lesson moves from the words to the pictures: C4 model levels, consistent notation for trust boundaries and data flow, and why a diagram that made sense with three engineers stops working once a team grows past that.
